messages.author: 945a91d0fe28fce8
messages.subject: Stan: Thank You
parts:
Greetings, I read the email thread below (my apology for a new thread but the email bounced back when I tried to respond from my workplace right now) and I wanted to comment before I head off for the long Holiday weekend here in the US.  During my 14+ year career as an applied statistician I have been on (and off) many user groups and IMHO this is one of the most informative user groups I have had the pleasure of "listening" to as I've have gained a lot of knowledge by the topics discussed by the users and Stan developers.  I am constantly amazed by the willingness and the extent of the Stan developers to consult via this group in a timely fashion and I am very grateful for your time.  To the entire Stan Development team, users who have posed interesting and thoughtful question, and any others I've failed to mention I would like to thank you and rest assured your time and consulting is truly appreciated.  Chuck

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

-----Original Message-----

From: stan-...@googlegroups.com [mailto:stan-...@googlegroups.com] On Behalf Of Bob Carpenter

Sent: Friday, September 02, 2016 1:57 PM

To: stan-...@googlegroups.com

Subject: Re: [stan-users] Help?

 

I like not being the only bad cop any more.  Go Daniel and Michael!

Now maybe we need to hire a good cop :-)

 

Public consulting's time consuming, too, but hopefully more than one person can benefit.

 

Another thing to add is that I don't like being shown things on a non-disclosure basis, because I can't keep track of where I learned what.  I don't want to violate anyone's confidentiality, so I simply try to avoid looking at anything that involves non-disclosure.  That includes turning down lots of paid consulting gigs and invitations to talks that require NDAs.  I'll almost never sign an NDA or a non-compete.  As Michael said, I came to this position because I like working in the open and got tired of NDAs after ten years of being in industry.

 

And thanks for asking first.  I really don't want people sending me things and then asking me not to share them.  I go through them too fast and might inadvertently forward them or disclose something I shouldn't without even realizing it.

 

- Bob

 

> On Sep 2, 2016, at 7:40 PM, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:

>

> Just to play bad cop a bit — I think everyone on the Stan team came to

> their current positions because they want to help scientists to better

> science, but it’s _really_ hard to do that without seeing the models

> and the data.  There’s just too much that can go wrong, so if the

> generic advice in the manual hasn’t been helpful then there’s not too

> much more that we can do.

>

> We are sympathetic to the sensitivity of the results, but honestly

> private consulting is very time consuming and without proper

> collaboration (including input on the model and co-authorship) it’s

> hard to motivate such help when we could be helping so many more

> people with open problems.

>

> Given the constraints I think that your most promising approach right

> now is to try to identifying parts of the model that might be causing

> issues, and abstract those away to examples that you can share

> publicly.  It is so much easier to answer specific questions with

> example models.

>

> On Sep 2, 2016, at 6:12 PM, FB <fb...@cam.ac.uk> wrote:

>

>> Hi Daniel and Bob,

>>

>> Many thanks for your quick replies.

>>

>> To Daniel: I have been playing a lot with re-parametrizations of the model. For example I have a multivariate normal prior (with known covariance matrix) on some of my parameters: I started by using the covariance matrix formulation but I had a lot of divergent transitions and in that case increasing adapt_delta (to 0.99) did not solve the problem. I then found that parametrizing in terms of the precision (rather than the covariance matrix) leads to very little divergent transitions (0/1/2 depending on the seed), in this case I have not tried increasing adapt_delta but I guess it would help even though it would also make the model even slower (it takes approximately 6h for 2000 iterations now). Concerning non-centered re-parametrization I have read the manual, however my observations are Poisson distributed so I do not know how to re-parametrize in such case.

>>

>> To Bob: I understand your point and I understand that private questions are not a priority. However, after discussion with my advisor, we concluded that it is not a good idea to make the model public yet. If we get the model to work and the issues I encounter can help other people, we are very happy to make it public later. I have a commented version of the code along with some modeling notes that I wrote to clarify what the codes do that I could share if you can help me.

>>

>> Thank you

>> Fran

>>

>> On Friday, September 2, 2016 at 4:28:23 PM UTC+1, FB wrote:

>> Hi,

>>

>> Thank you for developing STAN. I am currently doing a PhD and I have been using STAN to fit a multi-state back-calculation model to estimate age-specific HIV incidence.

>>

>> I wrote and ran the model, but I have occasional divergent transitions warnings and the model runs quite slowly (despite it mixes well), so I was wondering if you could help me with that.

>>

>> This model is the biggest part of my PhD work, so I am not entirely willing to put it on the mailing list. Would it be too much to ask to contact you, and send the codes, via email?

>>

>> Many thanks

>> F.

>>

messages.author: 3fe90052fbf2f899
messages.subject: Re: Stan: Thank You
parts:
I'd like to echo Chuck's appreciation.  This forum was a huge help during my dissertation, and I still glance through the topics a few times each week to read threads related to the issues I use Stan for.  The plurality of expertise among the contributors (some with pragmatic programming tricks, some (particularly Michael!) with great conceptual explanations of the underlying math that would otherwise make my head explode, some with decades of "field" experience, etc.) makes these email threads useful just to peruse and bookmark for later use.  Thanks so much to everyone here!

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
UvA web page: http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Stan: Thank You
parts:
Thanks much for the encouragement. This is why we want to
keep the discussions open.

As an aside, openness is why Andrew started blogging in the first
place. He said he was writing the same content to one person
at a time and decided he might as well share. Without writing
some posts asking questions on his blog, we wouldn't have gotten
some of the key advice we needed back when we first built Stan (like
to use autodiff and HMC!). Andrew's blog is also how Michael found
us while working in an online advertising shop after finishing a Ph.D.
in physics.

- Bob
